PMC Copyright notice PMCID: PMC12222039  PMID: 40620402 Abstract The plantar fascia is composed of fibrous connective tissue that forms a band running from the calcaneal tubercle distally to the toes. One of its main roles is to provide passive support to the medial longitudinal arch on the sole of the foot. This support is compared to a tie-rod tension producer during weigh

figures.caption: Figure 1. Open in a new tab Figure 1A: Transducer Placement on Plantar Fascia in Long Axis (LAX) To obtain a LAX view of the plantar fascia, the transducer is placed longitudinally along the plantar surface of the foot, starting at the medial calcaneal tuberosity and extending distally toward the metatarsal heads. Figure 1B: Transducer Placement on Plantar Fascia in Short Axis (SAX) To obtain a SAX view, maintain the same patient positioning and rotate the transducer perpendicular to the fascia’s fibers, typically just distal to the calcaneal insertion.

Figures 2A and 2B. Normal Plantar Fascia Insertion in LAX. Open in a new tab Refer to Figure 1A for the transducer position for this image. This view allows for detailed assessment of the fascia’s origin on the calcaneus, where it typically appears as a thick, hyperechoic, fibrillar band measuring approximately 3.5–4.0 mm in thickness and tapers as it moves anteriorly. The cortical surface of the calcaneus is identified as a continuous echogenic line with posterior acoustic shadowing and may show irregularities or enthesophyte formation in pathological cases. The calcaneal fat pad lies superficial to the fascia and appears as a lobulated, hypoechoic layer, helping to distinguish soft tissue planes. In more distal imaging, the underlying flexor digitorum brevis muscle may be visible. This view is ideal for identifying signs of plantar fasciitis, including fascial thickening, hypoechogenicity, and loss of normal fibrillar architecture at the insertion site.

Figures 3A and 3B. Normal Plantar Fascia Insertion in SAX. Open in a new tab Refer to Figure 1B for the transducer position for this image. The fascia appears as an oval-to-flat, well-defined hyperechoic structure centered over the medial calcaneal tuberosity. This orientation allows for the evaluation of fascial thickness, symmetry, and surrounding soft tissue. The central band is most prominent, but in some cases, medial and lateral slips may be visualized. Superficial to the fascia lies the dermis and subcutaneous fat, while deep to it, the curved echogenic line of the calcaneal cortex is visible. Pathological changes, such as focal thickening, asymmetry, or disruption of fascial borders, can be more clearly appreciated in this view. Additionally, surrounding fibrous septa and connective tissue can be examined for signs of edema or fascial strain, making this view a valuable complement to the LAX scan in comprehensive plantar fascia assessment.

Figure 4. Plantar Fasciitis with Calcifications, 4A LAX and 4B SAX. Open in a new tab The appearance of plantar fasciitis is typically characterized on MSK ultrasound by a thickened plantar fascia, most commonly measured at the medial calcaneal insertion, with a thickness exceeding 4.0 mm being suggestive of pathology. The normally hyperechoic, fibrillar pattern of the fascia becomes hypoechoic and heterogeneous, indicating inflammation and degeneration of the collagen matrix. There may also be loss of the normal sharp fascial borders, especially along the deep margin adjacent to the calcaneus. In chronic cases, enthesophytes (bony spurs and calcifications as shown above) may be visualized at the calcaneal origin, and increased Doppler signal within or around the fascia may reflect active inflammation. Assessment is most commonly performed using the LAX view, which provides a complete evaluation of the fascial origin, architecture, and cortical bone interface. The SAX view is helpful to assess fascial symmetry and surrounding soft tissue changes, such as perifascial edema.

Figure 5. Plantar Fasciitis with Small Rupture, 5A LAX and 5B SAX. Open in a new tab MSK ultrasound appearance of a plantar fascia tear shown above is identified by focal disruption of the normal fibrillar architecture, with an anechoic or hypoechoic gap within the fascial fibers, typically located near the calcaneal insertion but may also occur more distally. Partial tears often present as localized hypoechoic areas or clefts within a thickened or degenerated fascia, while complete ruptures may show complete discontinuity of the fascial band, sometimes with retraction of the torn ends. Associated findings may include fluid collection, perifascial edema, or hematoma in acute cases. The LAX view is essential for visualizing the extent of the disruption along the length of the fascia, while the SAX view helps confirm the width and depth of the defect, assess surrounding tissue involvement, and distinguish true tears from inflammatory changes. Both views are necessary for comprehensive evaluation and comparison to the contralateral side is often useful, especially in partial tears.

Figure 6. Plantar Fasciopathy with Medial Calcaneal Stress Fracture, 6A LAX and 6B SAX. Open in a new tab LAX and SAX ultrasound imaging of the plantar heel demonstrates a thickened plantar fascia at its calcaneal insertion, measuring greater than 4 mm, with hypoechoic changes and loss of the normal fibrillar architecture—findings consistent with plantar fasciopathy. Adjacent to the medial calcaneal tuberosity, there is cortical irregularity with adjacent periosteal elevation and hypoechoic marrow changes, suggestive of a medial calcaneal stress fracture. No significant fluid collection or full-thickness fascial tear is noted.
